Here are three short samples of my writing. Match my style in what you write.

making them play lame chicken.... Now all this done by a young lady who remembers eighteen months ago with so much regret that she has lost so much of her high spirits--might argue that her spirits were before tremendous; and yet they were not. That other Sarah was ladylike, I am sure, in her wildest moments, but there is something hurried and boisterous in this one's tricks that reminds me of some one who is making a merit of being jolly under depressing circumstances. No! that is not a nice Sarah now, to my taste.

The commencement of '61 promised much pleasure for the rest of the year, and though Secession was talked about, I do not believe any one anticipated the war that has been desolating our country ever since, with no prospect of terminating for some time to come. final_message:
We were to leave on Tuesday. The trunks were packed, the carriage ordered, and I had gone so far as to say my farewells to the hens, who received them with their usual indifference. And now, at the eleventh hour, all is undone by a single letter.

It came this morning, brought up from the village by a boy who evidently thought the news too heavy for his legs and dawdled accordingly. Aunt Maria is ill. Not dangerously, they say; but when did anyone ever write "not dangerously" of a thing they did not fear? Mother read it twice, folded it with great care, and announced that we should not go to the seaside at all, but to her. I thought it very good of her, and told her so. She said it was not goodness, only arithmetic: one sick sister, two idle daughters, and a house in want of both.

Idle! I who have hemmed six handkerchiefs this week alone!

I will confess, though, that I sulked a little. For months I had lived upon the thought of that sea. I had pictured myself upon the sand, hatless and unrebuked, with nobody to say that a young lady's complexion is not her own to squander. I had even rehearsed what I should say to the first wave. Now, in place of salt air, I am promised a sickroom, camphor, and Aunt Maria's cat, a creature who has hated me since the year 'fifty-nine and has never once pretended otherwise.

How quickly one's whole heart can be turned about! At breakfast I was a traveller; by dinner I was a nurse. I am not sure I like the change of costume. And yet, when I think of poor Aunt Maria lying alone, listening to the clock and wondering whether anyone will come, the sea seems a very selfish thing to want. It will be there next summer. She, perhaps, will not.

So the trunks are being unpacked, and the bathing-dress laid back in its drawer with something very like a sigh. Sister declares I am being tragic. Perhaps I am. But I notice she has not offered to carry the camphor.

We start at dawn. I shall take my sewing, my patience, and, if I can find it in time, a small stick for the cat.
